transcript.content: Hello. I'm glad you're here today. What brings you in to see me?

Hi doctor. I’m here because I can’t sit through long production meetings or edit sessions anymore—I keep getting up and pacing even when I know I should stay in my seat. It's starting to really impact my career as a camera operator and editor, especially since I'm trying to move into a senior role.
Have you struggled with this kind of restlessness and difficulty staying seated since you were a child, or is this a newer pattern that started in adulthood?

This isn't a new issue; it actually dates back to my childhood. Even in elementary school, teachers constantly told my parents that I couldn't stay in my seat and was always getting up to sharpen my pencil or wander around while other kids worked. It's always been there, but it has only recently become a major problem for my career with these long meetings.
Do you find that this restlessness is driven by constant, uncontrollable worry about various aspects of your life, or is it more of a physical urge to move without feeling anxious?

It’s definitely a physical urge rather than worry or anxiety. I get this crawling, pent-up energy in my body, almost like I'm in the wrong gear, and I physically feel so wound up that I just have to get up and move. Even on my days off when I’m just trying to relax on the couch, I can’t sit still for more than ten minutes before I have to get up and do something.
Along with this physical restlessness, do you also frequently struggle with maintaining focus, making careless mistakes, or getting easily distracted during your work or daily tasks?

Yes, I definitely do. On tight deadlines, I often make careless mistakes like missing obvious color notes or typos in lower thirds because I skimmed too fast, which forces me to re-export cuts. Also, during production meetings, I'll completely drift off thinking about shot ideas and have to ask people to repeat themselves, even though I was looking right at them.
Do you also find yourself acting impulsively, such as blurting out answers before a question is finished, interrupting others, or struggling to wait your turn?

Yes, and it's honestly pretty embarrassing. On set or in meetings, I have a bad habit of cutting people off and blurting out suggestions before they've even finished explaining the problem. I also find myself jumping into other people's conversations at festivals or leaning over a colleague's shoulder to comment on their edit uninvited, and afterward I always worry I came off as really rude or pushy.
You mentioned these challenges started in elementary school. Do you recall if these symptoms of restlessness and inattention were already clearly noticeable before you turned 7 years old?

I can't recall the exact age or if it was precisely before I turned seven, but it was definitely happening early on in elementary school. I vividly remember teachers complaining to my parents that I was constantly getting up to sharpen my pencil or wandering the classroom while everyone else was sitting quietly.

latest_inference.note: The patient meets the clinical criteria for Hyperkinetic Disorder / ADHD, showing prominent symptoms of both inattention (careless mistakes, drifting off, difficulty sustaining focus) and hyperactivity-impulsivity (restlessness, inability to remain seated, blurting out, interrupting). These symptoms have been present since early childhood (elementary school), occur across multiple settings (work, home, social), and cause significant impairment. Other causes, such as anxiety, have been ruled out. Therefore, the candidates F90.0 (Disturbance of activity and attention) and F90.9 (Hyperkinetic disorder, unspecified) remain highly appropriate, and we can finalize the assessment.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets the diagnostic criteria for F90.0 (Disturbance of activity and attention / ADHD, combined type). They present with a long-standing history dating back to early childhood of both significant inattention (careless mistakes, difficulty sustaining attention in meetings) and hyperactivity/impulsivity (inability to remain seated, constant physical restlessness, interrupting others, and intruding on conversations). These symptoms are pervasive across multiple settings (work and home) and cause clear functional impairment in their career progression.
